caption_hook: New Jersey has a hidden lake of water, a first-ever dinosaur skeleton and glowing rocks in the north.

layers.name: COHANSEY SAND
layers.hook: The sponge under the Pine Barrens
layers.what: Beaches and rivers once laid down thick, clean sand across southern New Jersey. Today that sand soaks up rain like a giant sponge and feeds the pine forests above.
layers.bonus: The Kirkwood-Cohansey aquifer under the Pine Barrens holds about 17.7 trillion gallons.

layers.name: WOODBURY FORMATION
layers.what: Shallow-sea muds in South Jersey covered a dinosaur's bones. They were dug from a marl pit in Haddonfield in 1858, giving us Hadrosaurus, a duck-billed dinosaur.
layers.bonus: Its skeleton, mounted in 1868, is called the first dinosaur ever displayed this way.

layers.name: PALISADES SILL
layers.what: Magma squeezed between layers of rock as the Atlantic began to open and cooled into a thick sheet of diabase. Erosion has carved it into the steep cliffs facing New York City.
layers.bonus: The Palisades cliffs rise more than 500 ft above the Hudson River.

layers.name: SHAWANGUNK FORMATION
layers.hook: Pebbles of a lost mountain range
layers.what: Rivers poured quartz pebbles and sand off ancient mountains into a vast plain. Cemented into very hard conglomerate, it caps the high ridges of northwest New Jersey.
layers.bonus: It makes up High Point, the state's highest spot at 1,803 ft.

layers.name: FRANKLIN MARBLE
layers.what: Ancient seafloor limestone was baked into marble that hosts zinc ore and over 350 different minerals. About 90 of them glow brightly under ultraviolet light.
layers.bonus: Franklin and Ogdensburg are famous worldwide as fluorescent mineral capitals.
